newsitem.title: USA: Miami declares fiscal emergency, fires auditor.
newsitem.headline: Miami declares fiscal emergency, fires auditor.

text.p: The Miami City Commission declared a fiscal emergency Monday, citing a budget gap of $68 million for fiscal 1997, which began Oct. 1.

The city commission also voted unanimously to dismiss outside auditor Deloitte & Touche LLP, and accused the accounting firm of failing to provide adequate warning about the city's budget problems. The commission also said it will investigate possible legal action against the firm.
The emergency declaration will allow the city to reopen contracts with its four employee unions.
Acting City Manager Merrett Stierheim said the city would first seek voluntary concessions of $15 million, or 10 percent of union payroll, before attempting to reopen contracts.
He said the city would also seek to raise fees by $14 million, to cut services by $3 million and seek pension cost reductions of $6 million to help offset the budget shortfall.
He said the city would also explore lease-back agreements, federal and state grants and the sale of unneeded assets to help close the budget gap.
Stierheim said the $68 million figure was based on "a very preliminary analysis" and warned commissioners that "It could change substantially."
The commission authorized him to hire certified public accountants to help review the city's recorss and internal budget controls, which Stierheim described as "slim to non-existant."

Stierheim was appointed after the resignation of City Manager Cesar Odio, who faces federal bribery charges in connection with an alleged kickback scheme involving city contracts. City Finance Director Manohar Surana, who controlled both finance and budget operations, also resigned and has agreed to plead guilty in the case.

Commissioners said they did not learn until after the resignations that the budget Surana submitted, and which they adopted, was not balanced. By then it was too late to raise property taxes for the year.

Asked by commssioners why they had not issued a warning about the city's condition, Deloitte & Touche officials said that the financial statement they prepared for fiscal 1995 clearly noted that the city had a $26 million budget gap for that year, which ended Sept 30, 1995.

Frank Parades, who headed the firm's audit, told the commission that he submitted the document to the former finance director on March 30, 1996. But commissioners insisted they had never seen the document until a few days ago.
"The information has been there," Parades told the commission. "If your previous administration did not provide them to you, there's nothing we can say."

Parades said the firm had not begun its audit for fiscal 1996, which ended Sept 30, because the city would not close the books on that year for two or three more months. He also said the firm had not conducted any interim monitoring because the city had never asked it to.
"That's probably one of our problems," retored Commissioner J.L. Plummer.
Deloitte & Touche officials left the meeting after the questioning. They were not present when the commission voted to fire them, and could not immediately be reached for comment by telephone.
